title: Simple Logic
hook: The first answer feels quick because it skips the one step that would expose it.
counterintuition: Simple logic is not about doing harder math. It is about pausing when the intuitive answer arrives too smoothly and forcing the missing relation into view.
tryThisNow: Before accepting one quick answer, write the two quantities it compares and ask which one changes when the other changes.
keyTakeaway: When the easy answer arrives instantly, slow down long enough to test the relation it skipped.

breakdown.fastRead:
The route map on Hanna's pension app desk shows a default saving rate of 8 percent. A product lead says raising it to 10 adds only two percent, so users will barely notice. Hanna marks CRT on the map and writes the simple logic: two points is a 25 percent increase from eight.

The intuitive answer often grabs the visible number and stops. It sees “two” and misses “two out of eight.” Simple logic asks for the relation, not the first number that feels available.

A quick answer can be wrong because it is incomplete.
breakdown.deepRead:
The route map matters because the product team is not being foolish. The 8-to-10 change looks small on the screen. It is two points, and two feels light. Hanna slows the room by naming the base: if a worker saves 8 percent now, a move to 10 percent raises contributions by a quarter. The user's paycheck may feel that.

Simple logic fails when the mind answers a neighboring question. How big is the visible change? Two. How big is the change relative to the base? Twenty-five percent. Those are different questions, but the first one often shows up first and sounds complete. The correction is to state the relation out loud: compared with what, added to what, taken from what, over what time?

The missing relation is the trap.

Claude sees the same problem in an ambulance night-shift review. An invoice stack shows that one crew logged twice as many late arrivals after adding a second vehicle. The intuitive answer is that the vehicle failed. Claude marks simple logic on the invoice stack and checks call volume. The area handled three times as many calls, so late arrivals per call improved.

This is why reflection matters. It is not slow thinking for its own sake. It is a small brake on the first answer: translate the sentence, write the base, reverse the comparison, or test one simple case. If the answer survives that pause, use it. If it breaks, the pause paid for itself.
breakdown.fullRead:
The dashboard printout in Isla's architecture studio shows a renovation estimate: the new lobby wall costs 20 percent less if built in two phases. The contractor says the choice is obvious. Isla hears the intuitive answer forming and marks intuitive answer on the printout. Then she writes the missing relation: two phases reduce material waste but add three weeks of rent on temporary space.

Shane Frederick's work on Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making used short questions that lure people toward an immediate answer. The famous bat-and-ball style problem is not hard because the arithmetic is advanced. It is hard because the first answer feels fluent enough to stop reflection. The test asks whether you can distrust a smooth answer for ten seconds.

Try this question in ordinary form: what number did the first answer ignore?

You use that question at a watch retailer. Poppy holds a caliper beside a waitlist for a limited watch. The owner says a ten-percent deposit is harmless because it is only ten percent. But the deposit is nonrefundable and tied to a watch whose delivery date is uncertain. Poppy marks reflection on the caliper and compares the deposit with the buyer's walk-away cost, not the retail price alone.

Simple logic also prevents public numbers from fooling decent people. Manuel is reviewing vaccine-statistic framing with a visitor badge clipped to the health department folder. A draft says side effects doubled after a booster. The raw count moved from one report to two in a tiny subgroup. Manuel marks Frederick on the badge and rewrites the page to show counts, denominator, and absolute risk beside the relative change.

The point is not to distrust every simple claim. A simple claim may be exactly right. The point is to distrust the feeling that the first simple claim is complete. Ask what relation it used. Ask what relation it skipped. A number can be true and still answer the wrong question. The pause is small; the error it catches can be large.

Jules sees the postmortem version in a viral chart fact-check. A sample tray from a water test sits beside a chart that says contamination fell by half. The chart compares two wells after one dry week. Jules marks simple on the tray and rebuilds the fact-check around the full sampling period, because the clean-looking ratio ignored season and site count.

When the easy answer arrives instantly, slow down long enough to test the relation it skipped.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Simple Logic helps readers catch fluent wrong answers. They learn to pause, name the base, and check the relation before using a quick answer.

questions.prompt: After simple-logic risk surfaces, a renovation contractor says a two-phase wall build saves 20 percent on material, but the phased plan adds three weeks of temporary rent, what should the client see?

questions.explanation: The intuitive answer uses the clean material number. Simple logic asks whether that number answers total cost after the added weeks.

questions.prompt: Two simple-logic signals compete: a delivery dashboard says a route is “30 percent faster,” but it compares a Sunday trial with weekday traffic. What should be checked before changing routes?
choices: Whether the route is faster under the same day and traffic conditions.
Trial weekday traffic supports a narrower read of signals compete delivery; keep dashboard says route central and leave percent faster sunday aside.
Traffic what checked points toward a quicker call on delivery dashboard says; let simple-logic signals compete stand until sunday trial weekday contradicts it.
questions.explanation: The missing relation is like-for-like timing. The percentage may be true for Sunday and still wrong for weekday routing.
questions.whyItMatters: Simple Logic makes the delivery dashboard evidence look cleaner than it is, risking a delivery dashboard mistake in this setting. The answer protects delivery dashboard by asking for whether the route is faster under the same day and traffic conditions.

reviewCards.front: A quick number feels obvious. What should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask what relation the number uses: compared with what, out of what, over what time. The first answer often skips that relation.

reviewCards.front: Why does a true percentage still mislead?
reviewCards.back: It can answer the wrong comparison. Add counts, denominator, time frame, or base rate before using it.

reviewCards.front: What is the practical lesson of the CRT?
reviewCards.back: Distrust a smooth first answer for a few seconds. Write the relation it assumes and test one simple case before acting.

reviewCards.front: A cost saving excludes a required add-on. What is the simple logic move?
reviewCards.back: Move from visible saving to net cost. The relevant relation includes the add-on because the decision includes the add-on.

reviewCards.front: A chart looks simple and clean. What is the hidden risk?
reviewCards.back: It may be simple because the key relation was removed. Check period, denominator, comparison group, and conditions.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use a brief reflection pause when the first answer arrives too smoothly. Name the relation, write the base, and check whether the visible number answers the real question.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a percentage sounds decisive, then I will translate it into counts and denominator before using it.
If a saving is presented alone, then I will add required costs and compare net value.
If a raw count rises or falls, then I will check the rate against workload or volume.
If a chart is unusually clean, then I will ask what period, group, or condition was left out.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one quick answer in a meeting or message. Write the base it uses and one relation it might have skipped.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, collect three percentages or raw counts from reports and rewrite each as a full comparison.
